report.headline: Projected to a below-average NBA role after a two-year gap, with a usage forecast that beats naive baselines but a shooting forecast that does not

projection.text: The model projects a 15.5% usage rate in the NBA, below the league average of 20.0% (SD 5.2%) and below the 15.0% a simple 0.75x-of-production rule would suggest; the 80% interval runs from 10.3% to 20.7%, spanning roughly two-fifths of the league's usage spread.

risks.text: Projected usage of 15.5% falls well short of both the NBA average (20.0%) and the z-preservation baseline of 19.9%, implying a materially smaller offensive role than the subject's standing in the G League would suggest on its own.
The fitted slope for usage rate is only 0.529, meaning historically only about half of a player's relative standing in the G League carries over to NBA usage for this transition type.

The 95% interval for usage rate is wide, from 7.5% to 23.5%, nearly the full plausible range for an NBA rotation player, reflecting substantial individual-level uncertainty even though the model ranks players usefully in aggregate.

Two full seasons elapsed between the source G League season and the NBA move, and the estimate rests on only 45 historical GL->NBA transitions, both of which widen the uncertainty around applying this projection to an individual case.

strengths.text: In the source G League season, the subject produced 17.54 points and 10.859 rebounds per 75 possessions over 1,525 minutes across 50 games, with a usage rate of 19.9% that was almost exactly league-average (-0.02 sd).
True shooting in the source season was 57.3%, +0.36 sd above the G League average, suggesting above-average scoring efficiency prior to the move.

The players who historically made this exact GL->NBA transition sat +0.27 sd above their own league's average before moving, and the fitted slope for true shooting (0.798) is high, meaning a large share of standing typically carries across for this metric — though as noted, the model's shooting forecast is not itself trustworthy for this bundle.

uncertainty.text: The usage projection carries real information: its out-of-fold error of 3.3% beats the best trivial baseline's 4.3% over 367 held-out transitions. The true shooting projection does not: its out-of-fold error of 4.7% is no better than the trivial league-mean baseline's 4.7%, so the 53.9% true shooting figure should not be treated as informative despite its stated 80% interval of 48.1% to 59.8%.
